# Why Aengus is spelled that way — and what it costs to get it right

There is a version of this name the early internet had to settle for: *aengus*. This is the file on how **Aengus** replaced it.

Aengus's mythology is a study in winning without fighting. The three great set-pieces — his birth inside a stopped day, his taking of the Brug, and the dream-quest for Caer Ibormeith — are all victories of time: time held still, time parsed, time waited out. Cath Maige Tuired and Tochmarc Étaíne add the counselor and the host: the son whose wit saves his father, and the keeper of the Brug who shelters Étaín when the whole of Ireland has no safer room.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Aengus
- **ASCII form:** aengus
- **Meaning:** "One vigor, true strength"
- **Domain of influence:** Love, Youth, Poetry
- **Pantheon:** Celtic
- **Classification:** Tier 2
- **Original script:** —
- **Series:** The Restoration Files, No. 6 of 406

## The Name Before the Marks


Spoken, the name runs `/ˈoːŋ.ɡus/` — 'OHN-gus' — one long open 'oh', the ng of 'singer', a hard g, and a short unstressed 'us'. Modern Irish Aonghus and Scottish Aonghas have worn it toward 'AYN-guhs' — the Anglicized Angus.

## The Temple That Stands Now

The restored name is not a plaque; it is an address. The temple of **Aengus** lives at [/aengus/](/aengus/), with its mythology in the [lore halls](/aengus/lore/), its peer-reviewed record in the [Scholarly Edition](/aengus/scholars/), and its place in the pattern atlas on the [patterns floor](/aengus/patterns/).

The restoration keeps one feature the ASCII form drops. One is enough to matter, and the label says so plainly: Tier-2.

## Where the Name Stood First

Aengus is a textual god — no ogham stone names him and no votive inscription invokes him — but his mythic address is the single most famous piece of prehistoric architecture in Ireland. Brú na Bóinne, the palace of the Boyne, is a UNESCO World Heritage landscape, and the passage tomb of Newgrange (c. 3200 BCE), older than Stonehenge and the pyramids, has been identified with the tales' síd in Broga, Óengus's Brug, since the medieval topographical tradition. The mound's roof-box, which admits the rising sun into the chamber on the mornings around the winter solstice, was excavated and documented by Michael J. O'Kelly (1962–1975), who observed the phenomenon in 1967 — a real alignment behind the mythology of a god born of a stopped sun. The witnesses to the texts are exact: Tochmarc Étaíne is preserved in the twelfth-century Lebor na hUidre and later manuscripts; Aislinge Óenguso survives in the fifteenth-century British Library MS Egerton 1782, the basis of Shaw's edition. For the comparative figure, the material record is Romano-British: altars dedicated to Apollo Maponus from the military north, including the Corbridge series, with the Ravenna Cosmography's locus Maponi completing the map of the Divine Son's cult — comparative evidence, never identification. The temple on the web is the newest of these addresses — the first one that fits in a pocket.

## The Archetype at Work

The [pattern atlas](/patterns/) seats this temple in **3 industries**, each match argued and weighted: **Love, Dating & Relationships** (óengus Óg, the Irish love-god — the four birds of his kisses.); **Music, Arts & Performance** (the kisses that become birds singing around lovers' heads — love as performance.); **Sleep & Recovery Technology** (aislinge Óenguso — the dream in which he falls in love with a girl he has never met.). The [Resonance File](/aengus/blog/resonance/) reads those seats through the myths themselves.
